name: BOMA International on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Data Centers, Robots and Agentic AI
title: BOMA International on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Data Centers, Robots and Agentic AI
answer: BOMA International, the Building Owners and Managers Association, publishes boma.org, a resource library for commercial property owners and managers. Its AI coverage spans an agentic AI white paper, robots in property management, AI data centers and medical real estate. The most useful single item is the agentic AI white paper, which describes systems that act without human intervention, handling maintenance requests, scheduling repairs, screening residential applicants, managing tenant communications and predicting equipment failure to trigger preventive maintenance.

sections.body: BOMA International, the Building Owners and Managers Association, publishes boma.org as a resource library for commercial real estate owners and managers. The pages reviewed are articles and resource listings rather than one single report: a piece on the AI data center revolution, a piece on robots and other technologies changing the property manager's role, a piece on the resurgence of ambulatory surgery centers and what it means for medical real estate, and a listing for a white paper titled Agentic AI and the Future of Real Estate: Evolution and Implementation. The site was read on 1 October 2026, and the material reviewed does not state publication dates for the individual items.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Across the pages reviewed, BOMA treats AI both as a tool for building operations and as a force reshaping the property types its members own. The agentic AI white paper is described as defining agentic AI, tracing its evolution and sharing implementation strategies, and it says AI agents will move far beyond simple automation to execute complex tasks proactively without human intervention, handling maintenance requests, scheduling repairs, screening residential applicants, juggling routine tenant communications and alerting management to preventive maintenance needs by estimating when equipment will fail. An article on robots and property managers concludes that robots performing basic management tasks are still many years from broad implementation, because people prefer dealing with people, and notes that half the robots in a Japanese hotel were removed for that reason. Building security is called the most promising near-term application, with Knightscope and Allied Universal deploying patrol robots that use thermal imaging and license plate recognition. The data center article covers power density, liquid cooling and a technician shortage, while the medical real estate article describes AI as an integral tool for data collection, entry and analysis and reports that robotics are to the surgeon's hands as AI is to the surgeon's brain.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The article on AI data centers says they are five to ten times more power dense than traditional data centers, citing Sean Farney of JLL, and that data center electricity consumption is projected to more than double by 2030, citing Scientific American. It reports, citing Inova, that direct-to-chip cooling can remove 70 to 75 percent of the heat generated in a rack, leaving 25 to 30 percent for air cooling, and, citing Pittsburgh Public Source, that a large-scale data center in Western Pennsylvania would bring 80 to 100 long-term jobs. The medical real estate article says ambulatory surgery centers generated $45 billion in revenue in 2024, projected to reach $57 billion by 2030, citing Healthcare Finance News. The robots article notes that half the robots in a Japanese hotel were eliminated.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in commercial real estate would use these pages to see how an established owners and managers association frames the technology. The agentic AI white paper is the clearest statement of where operations are heading, describing agents that act on maintenance, leasing inquiries and tenant communication without a person in the loop. The robots article sets a realistic near-term horizon, pointing to security and lobby functions rather than full building management. The data center and medical office pieces show AI reshaping the demand side of commercial property, from power and cooling requirements to clinical and outpatient facilities, which matters to owners weighing what to build and how to service it.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The material is a resource library rather than original research, and much of it summarizes third-party reporting and interviews, including items from Scientific American, JLL, Inova, Healthcare Finance News and Becker's. Several pieces concern adjacent property types, data centers and medical outpatient facilities, rather than core office, retail or industrial operations. The agentic AI item is a listing for a white paper, so the detail available on the page is a summary rather than the full document. The pages reviewed do not state publication dates, and the publisher is a membership association whose framing reflects the interests of commercial building owners and managers.
